study.title: Numbers 5 - Prediction of the camp, repair of damage and marital fidelity
study.overview: Numbers 5 organizes the life of the people of Israel around the holiness of the Lord who dwells among them. The chapter brings together three themes related to each other: the removal of ritually impure people from the camp, the restitution when someone harms the neighbor and the law that deals with the suspicion of adultery. In all cases, the focus is not only social discipline, but the protection of divine holiness, personal responsibility before God and the preservation of the community order. The chapter shows that uncleanness, unrighteousness, and conjugal infidelity are not isolated matters: all touch the communion of the people with the Lord.

outline.title: Purification of the camp
outline.explanation: The Lord orders the unclean to be removed from the camp, including people with skin diseases, with discharge and those who touched a dead man. The stated reason is to prevent the presence of impurity from contaminating the place where God dwells in the midst of the people. Israel's immediate obedience shows that the holiness of the camp is treated as a community priority.

outline.title: Restitution and priestly portion
outline.explanation: If anyone sins against another person, he must confess the guilt, fully repair the damage and add a fifth to the value. If there is no relative to whom to return, compensation is given to the Lord by means of the priest, along with the guilt offering. The text also states that the holy things brought to the priest belong to him, showing a definite order for priestly sustenance and administration of the sacred.

outline.title: The woman's proof of suspicion of adultery
outline.explanation: When a husband, without direct witness, feels jealousy and suspicion of his wife, the case is taken to the priest. The woman passes through a solemn rite with barley offering, holy water mixed with dust from the tabernacle and an oath with curse. If there is guilt, the punishment will come; if it is clean, it will be free and will be in a favorable situation. The procedure declares that the husband is not guilty in taking the case, and that the woman will bear his own guilt if he has betrayed.

study.context: The notes provided understand this chapter as part of a set of laws aimed at the purity of Israel, the priesthood and the tabernacle. The setting is the camp of the people around the presence of God, so that matters of ritual impurity, moral damage and conjugal fidelity have religious weight, not just social or sanitary. The commentators cited note that in the ancient world such rules helped to preserve the identity of Israel as a people under God's rule and to prevent the holiness of the Lord from being treated with contempt.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter teaches that the holiness of God requires separation from what contaminates, reparation of offenses and relational integrity. The purity of the camp is not mere formalism: it testifies that God dwells in the midst of his people. Restitution shows that sin against others is also sin against the Lord, and therefore requires confession and concrete compensation. The law of jealousy, in turn, places the truth of the conjugal relationship before God, showing that suspicions and concealments do not escape his judgment. At the same time, the text preserves a concern with justice: the husband is not automatically guilty of bringing the matter, and the woman is treated for a formal procedure, not by mere private suspicion. For an evangelical reading, the chapter highlights the seriousness of sin, the need for atonement and the centrality of faithfulness before God.

scholarViews.insight: The expulsion of the unclean camp is presented as a measure to preserve God's holiness among the people, not just as a matter of hygiene or health.
The purity of the community must be as carefully preserved as its order and its peace; therefore, the unclean ones are removed until they are purified.
The refund must include not only the principal, but also an increase of one-fifth, strengthening the complete repair of the offense.

questions: What does this chapter teach about the relationship between personal holiness and community life before God?
In what ways does the restitution in Numbers 5:5-10 show that sin against one's neighbor is also sin against the Lord?
How does the law of jealousy confront both suspicion without proof and the real possibility of infidelity within marriage?
study.practice: Apply this chapter by examining three areas: purity before God, reparation of damage and fidelity in relationships. If there is sin or injury caused to someone, confess and seek to repair concretely, without minimizing the offense. If there are suspicions, treat them responsibly and honestly, avoiding hasty judgments. And throughout community life, value God's holiness as something that shapes words, decisions and relationships.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not explain in detail the exact meaning of some expressions of the rite of the bitter waters, nor do they allow to affirm with absolute certainty the physical nature of the punishment described. It is also not possible, based on these notes, to determine all the historical aspects of the procedure beyond what the text itself and the commentators say. Adam Clarke's reading of the body effect at 5:22 and 5:31 is interpretive, not an indisputable conclusion of the text.
